Yes 'A Spacetime Odyssey' was somewhat interesting with great visuals, but (and maybe this is because one of my majors is philosophy/ I am pretentious myself) the philosophical ideas (evolution/ zarathustra/ artificial intelligence etc.) for which this movie is partly lauded really aren't that great. It felt as if I was watching a potato being filmed from different angles, and it being praised as some genius marvel of profundity.

On the Shining I fully agree with Stephen King, who hated it, when he said: "In the book, there's an actual arc where you see this guy, Jack Torrance, trying to be good, and little by little he moves over to this place where he's crazy. And as far as I was concerned, when I saw the movie, Jack was crazy from the first scene." Kubrick movies but especially the Shining seem incredibly butchy, with the feeling that somehow scenes are lacking to explain for what without those scenes seem sudden jumps in character arcs or storyline, while also not being able to directly provoke questions that instead cowardly* lie concealed in plain-sight-mystery, knowing that snobs would see more into his films than there actually is. To put it more controversially and harshly (although I am less certain of this), I think it is likely Kubrick and his fans abuse (*hence cowardly) mystery to evoke a sense of grandeur and profundity. While the monolith in A Spacetime could signify a door to the next step in evolution, a screen itself or something else, it also could have been put in there to get people to wonder what it is.

To take away what I think you many of you suspect is the reason I don't like these films: I do thoroughly enjoy Bergman films and Satantango is one of my highest rated movies ever. Secondly, not all of Kubrick's films were unenjoyable: I ranked Paths of Glory and Full Metal Jacket with about a 8/10 each, while I gave A Spacetime 7/10 and The Shining 6/10. How do you rank his films?
I think Stanley Kubrick is a great filmmaker, (and a bit insane), but I don't consider him to be a good story teller.

I don't agree with Stephen King on his take on The Shining. I don't think it's a fair assessment to say that he doesn't have an arc. It just doesn't play out so plainly and steadily as King would have done it himself. Given that the overwhelming subtext, drive, and motivation for Jack Torrance is his alcoholism, we get his baseline in the conversation between Wendy and the therapist when she explains that he injured Danny. Then he quit and hasn't had a drop since. I think what Kubrick plays off of though is that the alcoholic, even when not drinking, has that personality that is predisposed to get drunk. That the beast is always there and not only is waiting to be awakened, but is trying very hard to be awakened. So King wants this 'he's a nice fellow and then gets bad' arc, whereas Kubrick takes Jack as already a recovered alcoholic who has the darkness inside, but he's bottling it. And early Jack shows that. I think King's vision is just unrealistic, that he's a happy family man even though he has been an abusive alcoholic in the past. It's unfair to call him crazy in the first scene. He's both in control but showing us what lies underneath. There is very much a progression in his character, and it's subtle, powerful, rewatchable, and relatable. King prefers the arc to be broad and obvious, and I just don't agree with that.

I don't think you can say with certainty it was Jacks alcoholism that drove this story, without being able to justify for the previous horrors that took place in hotel. On the Shining the supernatural variable to me cheapens the movie. Instead of the dozens of theories that try to explain this 'complex' movie, it to me is far more plausible Kubrick intended to create a film in which it was possible to create dozens of theories in the first place. Jack being put in the 1921 picture, having Charles and Delbert Grady that look exactly alike in the film, a sixth-sense/ possessed Danny and 'the Shining' itself are ploys, abusing the unfalsifiable supernatural to create a sense of complexity the story can't provide on its own. Working in a normal movie you would have to justify behavior and progression through actual and noticable variables, such that it would be strange for a person to go completely insane on the basis of being alone for a while. By using the supernatural you can justify anything you want.

You might be right. But for me both the book and movie are a parable about alcoholism and the family, with the horror element added just because it's well-suited to the topic. Recovering (and non-recovering) alcoholics always talk about their demons, haunted past, and how it's not them, but rather the drunk, that always wants another drink. Like it's a supernatural presence. And I thought they did that expertly in the movie. The conversation with Lloyd the bartender was exactly the kind of rationalizing that people in that situation do.

And like I said, I think the progression is pure throughout the movie, and it fits that of an abusive alcoholic to a tee. I always thought that the point about him always being there was the idea that the mindset of the alcoholic is always there, even when they're sober. The demons and emotional baggage are always there just waiting to be let out by a couple drinks. And when Delbert says that he has 'always been' there, and they show the picture at the end, I think the idea is that this wasn't just a singular phenomenon. That the whole thing isn't just craziness let out by a hotel. That it wasn't just a one-time lapse from drinking. That even when not drinking, he has always been there, with that mindset lurking. That it's always there.

And that's what leads to his breakdown at the end. In the hotel, he has no excuses for not becoming the fully-realized Jack that he could be. There are no excuses. He can't blame family obligations, he can't blame a hectic work schedule, or traffic, or distractions. He can't blame anyone else now. And he fails. And he descends on that spiral that familiar spiral, where he refuses to blame himself. Wendy comes in once, and he says that's the distraction. Then he gets that enabling drink from Lloyd and says that the situation with Danny wasn't really his fault. And the old family is holding him back. And that self pity becomes outward rage as he blames others for his failures. And there are stops along the way, of course. With some amazing scenes that mirror that alcoholic dynamic. Especially when he's holding Danny in his lap and asking him if he's okay. Perfect.

So anyway, I always read the book the same way that Kubrick put together the movie. That the supernatural is a metaphor for the demons of alcoholism. That the hotel is the alcoholic himself, where he's confronted with his own shortcomings and has no one or nothing else to blame. The demons were always there and he was always the caretaker. And the result of that inability to blame external forces causes that rage breakdown. It all mimics alcoholic behaviour exactly. As well as the destructive force of alcoholism on the household.

Anyway, that's how I watch the movie and it's one of my favorites. The pyschological horror is very real and palpable to me.

Then how do you explain the previous caretaker also killing his family with an axe? My explanation would be that he used that story to justify him murdering his own family. It gave him a way to not blame his desire to kill his family on his own shortcomings, but instead on the supernatural he and the person he got the job from suspected was the cause of the killings of the first tragedy. That'd still be difficult to reconcile with Danny being possessed, seeing things and being able to communicate through his mind with the black guy (who knew Dannys nickname was Doc without it ever being said.) that is very real. That would indicate inconsistencies on the part of Kubrick in his use of the hotel and the supernatural in what they precisely are.

Yeah, for Danny I never read anything into that. That that's part of the supernatural aspect of the story. It'd be burdensome to just make everything a heavy-handed alcoholism allegory without attempting to make a true horror movie as well. Danny with his supernatural powers is just a character. Stephen King usually works in a supernatural world and that works.

And the previous caretaker bit, yeah, just plays into the idea that this always happens, and it's going to happen again, and it has always happened. Sort of a universal cycle of violence. That when Grady tells him that he has always been the caretaker, that their violence is the same. I agree with you that Grady and his actions are justification/enabling, but less in the sense of supernatural compulsion and more in the idea that this hotel and Jack's tendencies are a state of mind that's all too common.

2001 did present the same things over and over. This was a deliberate choice on the part of Kubrick and Clarke meant to drive home the idea that we are on the cusp of the dawn of a totally new species. This is a huge fucking deal and people don't treat it with the respect that it deserves. There is only now anything like a mainstream awareness of the problems that might seriously come out of GAI and Kubrick/Clarke nailed the problems with value stability 45 years ago.

As for the Shining, I loved both Kubrick's and King's versions. Like a lot of King's stories, the lead character makes moral choices and, through his own failings, descends into his own hell. He is responsible for the results of his own actions. Kubrick takes a more clinical look at what happens when a weak person is placed in an extremely stressful situation. His Jack progresses quite naturally into insanity given his fragile mind and supernatural situation. It's clinical and detached and frightening because it suggests that there wasn't necessarily another decision that Jack could have made to prevent his fate.

I think he was a genius. His genius was to fully exploit his medium to produce exactly the message he wanted to convey. His messages are just never warm and personal and sometimes they're not very interesting (*cough* Barry Lindon *cough* Lolita *cough*), but they're always brilliantly executed.

Again, I think it's because Kubrick introduced those problems 1968 when those ideas weren't known to the public yet, combined with me having studied the topic prior to watching it that left me unimpressed. I never felt any mystery or 'mindfuck' while watching it.
